hints: Think about what sunlight provides that a cool dark cupboard does not, and why breaking a covalent bond needs that input.
Link the orange colour staying to whether any $\text{Br}_2$ is used up, and what particle must form first for hexane to react.
walkthrough:
Picture what must happen first**
Hexane is an alkane with strong $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{C-C}$ single bonds. It will not attack $\text{Br}_2$ on its own. For anything to happen, the $\text{Br-Br}$ bond has to split first to make very reactive $\text{Br}\cdot$ radicals.

See why darkness stops that first split**
Splitting $\text{Br-Br}$ evenly, called homolytic fission, needs a good input of energy from ultraviolet light. In the dark and kept cool, that energy is simply not available, so no $\text{Br}\cdot$ radicals form.

Connect to the observation**
With no radicals, there is no chain reaction and no $\text{Br}_2$ is consumed. That is why the mixture stays orange, the colour of unchanged bromine.

Final answer: No reaction occurs as there is insufficient energy for homolytic fission of $\text{Br}_2$.
No bromine free radicals are produced, so the orange colour of $\text{Br}_2$ remains.

hints: Recall the name given to the reaction where a hydrogen on an alkane is replaced by a halogen in UV light via radicals.
walkthrough:
Recognise the pattern**
You have an alkane plus bromine in sunlight, a hydrogen is swapped for bromine, and radicals are involved. That combination has one special name at AS level: free-radical substitution.
Final answer: Free-radical substitution

hints: In propagation the radical is used up and a new radical is made, so start with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$ plus $\text{Br}\cdot$ and think what $\text{H}$-containing small molecule can form.
walkthrough:
Build the hydrogen-stealing step**
A $\text{Br}\cdot$ radical is hungry for an electron. It collides with hexane, pulls off a hydrogen atom to form $\text{HBr}$, and leaves behind a new carbon radical $\cdot\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}$. One radical in, one radical out, so the chain continues: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14} + \text{Br}\cdot \rightarrow \cdot\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13} + \text{HBr}$$

hints: Now the carbon radical $\cdot\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}$ must react with a $\text{Br}_2$ molecule to give the organic product and reform a radical to keep the cycle going.
walkthrough:
Build the bromine-transfer step**
The $\cdot\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}$ radical attacks a $\text{Br}_2$ molecule. It takes one bromine atom to become 1-bromohexane, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{Br}$, and kicks out a fresh $\text{Br}\cdot$ radical. Again one radical is consumed and one is created: $$\cdot\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13} + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{Br} + \text{Br}\cdot$$

hints: Termination removes radicals completely, so join two radicals together with no $\cdot$ left on the right to make 1-bromohexane.
walkthrough:
Close the chain by joining radicals**
Termination is the opposite of propagation. Two radicals meet and pair their single electrons to make a normal covalent bond, so no radicals remain. To make 1-bromohexane directly, combine the two different radicals: $$\cdot\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13} + \text{Br}\cdot \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{Br}$$

hints: Hexane-1,2-diol has two $\text{OH}$ groups on carbons 1 and 2, so work backwards to where the $\text{C=C}$ bond must have been in the straight chain alkene.
walkthrough:
Map the diol back to the alkene**
Mild oxidation adds one $\text{OH}$ to each carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ bond. If the product is hexane-1,2-diol, the $\text{OH}$ groups are on C1 and C2, so the double bond must have been between C1 and C2.

Write the straight chain**
Put the double bond at the end of a six carbon chain: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$$ This is hex-1-ene. It cannot show cis-trans isomerism because C1 has two identical H atoms, which fits A does not show stereoisomerism.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ (hex-1-ene)

hints: Remember that hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$ cleaves the double bond, so think what milder temperature is needed to stop at the diol.
Recall the two other words always quoted with the $\text{KMnO}_4$ reagent for diol formation, describing its concentration and pH.
walkthrough:
Keep the oxidation gentle**
To stop at hexane-1,2-diol you need mild conditions. Heating or using concentrated reagent would break the carbon chain completely.

State the three classic conditions**
The standard recipe is cold, dilute and acidified potassium manganate(VII). All three are needed for full marks.
Final answer: Cold, dilute, acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$

hints: Focus on what happens to the $\text{C=C}$ bond when $\text{H}_2$ adds across it with a Pt catalyst.
walkthrough:
Classify adding hydrogen**
$\text{H}_2$ adds across the double bond in B to give the saturated hexane. Adding hydrogen across an unsaturated bond is called addition, which for hydrogen is also reduction.
Final answer: Addition (reduction)

hints: Start by counting the type of bonding in every $\text{C-C}$ link in hexane, which contains only single bonds.
Then compare with the $\text{C=C}$ double bond in alkene B, thinking how many $\sigma$ and how many $\pi$ components it contains.
walkthrough:
Describe hexane first**
Hexane is an alkane, so every $\text{C-C}$ link is a single bond. A single bond is always one $\sigma$ bond formed by direct head on overlap, with no $\pi$ bond present.

Describe alkene B**
B is an alkene, so it still has $\sigma$ bonds along the carbon skeleton, including one $\sigma$ bond between the two doubly bonded carbons. In addition, the $\text{C=C}$ double bond contains one extra $\pi$ bond from sideways p orbital overlap. That one $\pi$ bond is the key difference.

Final answer: Hexane contains only $\sigma$ bonds between carbon atoms.
B contains $\sigma$ bonds between carbons and one $\pi$ bond in the $\text{C=C}$ double bond.
